findings.claim: The 60 marks split three ways. Ten marks reward your statement of aims. Twenty marks reward how fully your production meets the requirements of the brief — completing every task, suiting the specified form and genre, and being appropriate for the target audience. Thirty marks, the largest single share, reward how well you use media language to communicate meaning and construct representations
findings.problem: Invented mark split. The Eduqas GCSE Media Studies specification (C680QS) awards Component 3 a maximum of 60 marks, assessed with two grids in Appendix A: the Statement of Aims (10 marks) and the media production (50 marks). The production's 50 marks are awarded holistically against band descriptors that cover both meeting the requirements of the set brief and the use of media language/representation; the specification nowhere splits them into 20 marks and 30 marks. A per-part mark split the specification does not state is a fabrication.
findings.correction: The 60 marks split two ways. Ten marks reward your statement of aims. The remaining fifty marks reward the production itself, judged as a whole: how fully it meets the requirements of the brief (completing every task, suiting the specified form and genre, and being appropriate for the target audience) and how well it uses media language to communicate meaning and construct representations, for example through camerawork, layout, editing or the way people and places are portrayed.

findings.claim: Match each mark allocation to what it assesses in the non-exam assessment. | 10 marks / 20 marks / 30 marks | Meeting the requirements of the set brief / Using media language to communicate meaning and construct representations / The statement of aims
findings.problem: The 20-mark and 30-mark allocations do not exist. The specification allocates 10 marks to the statement of aims and 50 marks to the media production, which is assessed on one grid covering brief requirements and media language/representation together. The question drills a fabricated mark breakdown.
findings.correction: Replace with an MCQ: 'How are the 60 marks for the non-exam assessment allocated?' Options: '10 marks statement of aims, 50 marks production' (correct); '20 marks statement of aims, 40 marks production'; '30 marks statement of aims, 30 marks production'; '10 marks statement of aims, 20 marks brief, 30 marks media language'.

findings.claim: How many marks reward meeting the brief's requirements? / 20 marks.
findings.problem: Fabricated figure. The specification does not award a separate 20 marks for meeting the brief; the whole production, including how far it meets the brief, is marked out of 50.
findings.correction: Q: How many marks are awarded for the media production itself? A: 50 marks, with the remaining 10 for the statement of aims.

findings.claim: How many marks reward the use of media language and representation? / 30 marks.
findings.problem: Fabricated figure. Use of media language and representation is assessed within the single 50-mark production grid in Appendix A of the specification, not as a separate 30-mark strand.
findings.correction: Q: Which two things does the 50-mark production grid reward? A: Meeting the set brief and using media language and representation effectively.

findings.claim: Markers reward specific, subject-terminology-rich statements that show real understanding of media language and representation, not just a summary of what your production is about.
findings.problem: Unevidenced claim about marker behaviour. The specification's statement of aims criteria require candidates to explain how they intend to apply knowledge and understanding of media language and representation and target the audience; it makes no claim about markers rewarding 'terminology-rich' writing, and the component carries no marks for written expression.
findings.correction: The statement of aims is assessed on how clearly it explains your intentions, so name the actual techniques you plan to use — which camera angles, colour schemes or codes of representation you intend to include — and how each one targets your audience, rather than simply summarising what your production is about.

findings.claim: All material must be original except an existing song without an official video; using non-original material caps your marks at band 2.
findings.problem: Loose wording that contradicts the exception stated in the same sentence. The specification's rule is that candidates who do not use original footage, images or text must not be awarded marks above band 2; permitted non-original music, credited on the cover sheet, does not cap the mark.
findings.correction: All footage, images and text must be original except a permitted existing song without an official video; failing to use original footage, images or text caps your production marks at band 2.

findings.claim: Section B uses <dfn class="term" ...>stepped questions</dfn> on media industries (Question 3) and audiences (Question 4).
findings.problem: The Eduqas GCSE Media Studies specification (C680QS) does not allocate Section B of Component 1 to a fixed 'Question 3 = industries, Question 4 = audiences' split. The specification states that Section B assesses two of the media forms studied (film, newspapers, radio, video games) and that the second question may assess knowledge and understanding of media industries, audiences OR media contexts. The fixed per-question topic allocation is an invented structural detail.
findings.correction: Section B uses <dfn class="term" data-def="A question broken into linked parts that build in mark tariff, usually moving from short recall to extended explanation.">stepped questions</dfn> on two of the media forms you have studied. One question assesses media industries; the other may assess media industries, audiences or media contexts, so you must revise all three areas for every Section B form.

findings.claim: {"q": "Which area does Question 4 in Section B assess?", "a": "Audiences."}
findings.problem: The specification does not fix the second Section B question to audiences; it states the question may assess media industries, audiences or media contexts. Telling students Question 4 is always an audiences question could lead them to under-revise industries and contexts for that question.
findings.correction: {"q": "Which three areas can the second stepped question in Section B assess?", "a": "Media industries, audiences or media contexts, depending on the paper."}

findings.claim: Question 1 always uses the command word ‘analyse’ and asks you to examine one set product through media language.
findings.problem: The specification describes the Section A media language question as a stepped question on one set product (with reference to relevant contexts possibly required); it does not guarantee a single undivided task or that the command word is always 'analyse'. Lower-tariff parts of a stepped question typically use 'identify', 'state' or 'explain'. The lesson also implies stepped questions occur only in Section B.
findings.correction: Question 1 assesses media language in relation to one set product and is stepped, so the earlier parts may use command words such as ‘identify’ or ‘explain’ before the highest-tariff part asks you to analyse how media language constructs meaning. Reference to relevant contexts may also be required.

findings.claim: Ignoring the command word is one of the most common ways marks are lost: an ‘analyse’ question rewarded only for description will not reach the top bands, no matter how much detail is included.
findings.problem: The first clause is an unevidenced claim about how candidates typically lose marks; no published board document states this frequency. The mark-scheme point (description alone cannot access the top bands of an analysis question) is supportable on its own.
findings.correction: The command word tells you which skill the mark scheme rewards: an ‘analyse’ question answered only with description cannot reach the top bands, no matter how much detail is included.

findings.claim: Examiners reward analysis of effect, not description of presence.
findings.problem: Unevidenced assertion about examiner behaviour. The assessment criteria reward analysis of how meaning is constructed; attributing this to what 'examiners reward' is not a claim the specification or published mark schemes make in these terms.
findings.correction: The higher bands are awarded for explaining the effect of a feature, not for noting that it is present.

findings.claim: Audience questions often reward theoretical perspectives such as Blumler and Katz’s Uses and Gratifications theory.
findings.problem: 'Often reward' is an unevidenced claim about exam frequency and examiner behaviour. Uses and gratifications is named in the specification content, but no board document states how often audience questions credit it or that theory is required to access higher bands.
findings.correction: Uses and gratifications theory (associated with Blumler and Katz) is named in the specification content for audiences, so it is legitimate to use. Listing the four needs (information, personal identity, integration and social interaction, and entertainment) is not enough on its own — apply one of them to a named set product and explain how the product satisfies it.

findings.claim: Textual analysis of their camerawork, layout or colour scheme earns no credit in this section — the focus is ownership, funding, regulation, targeting and audience response.
findings.problem: The specification states that Section B assesses media industries, audiences and media contexts in relation to the forms studied; it does not state that references to a product's textual features 'earn no credit'. Presenting an invented marking rule risks students discarding valid material (for example branding or house style used to illustrate an audience-targeting point).
findings.correction: The Section B set products are studied as examples of industry and audience issues, so detail about a product’s camerawork, layout or colour scheme only helps if it supports an industry, audience or context point — the focus here is ownership, funding, regulation, targeting and audience response.

findings.claim: Section B set products illustrate industry and audience issues only; textual analysis of their features earns no credit there.
findings.problem: Repeats the invented marking rule. The specification does not say textual detail earns no credit in Section B, and it also allows the second Section B question to assess media contexts, not only industries and audiences.
findings.correction: Section B set products are used to illustrate media industries, audiences and media contexts — keep textual detail only where it supports an industry, audience or context point.

findings.claim: Section A tests media language and representation through print media forms such as magazines, film posters, newspapers and print advertisements. Section B tests media industries and audiences through film, newspapers, radio and video games.
findings.problem: The specification states that each section assesses two of the listed forms in any given paper, even though all the set products are studied. As written, students may expect all four forms to appear in each section.
findings.correction: Section A tests media language and representation in relation to two of the print media forms you have studied (magazines, film posters, newspapers or print advertisements). Section B tests media industries and audiences in relation to two of the forms you have studied (film, newspapers, radio or video games) — so revise all of them, because you will not know in advance which two are set.

findings.claim: {"q": "What is the original broadcaster of the 1970s crime drama studied for comparison?", "a": "ITV."}
findings.problem: Out of scope. For this qualification's Component 2 Section A from 2027 the set television products are Trigger Point, Man Like Mobeen and Modern Family (the specification states one extract will be set from Luther in 2025 and 2026 or Trigger Point from 2027 onwards, one from Man Like Mobeen and one from Modern Family). There is no separately assessed '1970s crime drama studied for comparison' in the 2027 television set for this unit, so this card sends students to revise a product they will not be examined on.
findings.correction: {"q": "Which broadcaster first aired Trigger Point, the crime drama option set for Section A?", "a": "ITV."}

findings.claim: Name the original broadcaster of the 1970s crime drama studied for comparison with the contemporary crime drama option.
findings.problem: Out of scope for this unit. The television products set for Component 2 Section A from 2027 are Trigger Point, Man Like Mobeen and Modern Family; a 1970s crime drama is not a set television product students are examined on for this series, so practising it wastes revision time.
findings.correction: Name the broadcaster of the contemporary crime drama set for Section A (Trigger Point). [Correct answer: ITV. Any other answer scores no marks.]

findings.claim: Explain how differences in funding model between a 1970s crime drama extract and a contemporary crime drama extract might be reflected in their content and style.
findings.problem: Out of scope: the exam sets one extract from the studied contemporary television product (Trigger Point, Man Like Mobeen or Modern Family from 2027). Students will not be given a 1970s crime drama extract to compare, so the question rehearses a task that cannot appear.
findings.correction: Explain how the funding model of the broadcaster of your set television product might be reflected in its content and style. [Mark scheme wording unchanged, with examples drawn from the set product rather than from two extracts.]

findings.claim: Examiners reward this kind of joined-up answer, which is called a <dfn class="term" ...>synoptic</dfn> response.
findings.problem: Unevidenced claim about examiner behaviour. The specification does not describe Component 2 answers as 'synoptic' or state that examiners award extra credit for linking framework areas; it uses 'synoptically' about the non-exam assessment (Component 3), where knowledge is drawn together through practical production. The mark scheme criteria for Q1/Q3 are analysis, judgement and conclusions.
findings.correction: An answer that links these areas together is often called a joined-up or connected response: for example, explaining how a broadcaster's decision to air a programme on a particular channel (industry) shapes the kind of representation it can show (representation) and who is likely to watch it (audience).

findings.claim: Naming the four needs — information, personal identity, integration and social interaction, and entertainment — only earns limited credit on its own.
findings.problem: Unevidenced assertion about how marks are awarded. No published board document states a credit limit for naming Blumler and Katz's categories; the assessment criteria reward application of knowledge to the set products, but the specific 'limited credit' claim is invented.
findings.correction: Simply naming the four needs — information, personal identity, integration and social interaction, and entertainment — is not enough on its own: the criteria reward applying them to the set product.

findings.claim: The specification expects a more balanced argument: stereotypes also let audiences interpret media quickly
findings.problem: Attributes to the specification a requirement it does not state. The specification lists stereotyping as part of the study of representation but does not instruct candidates to argue both sides. The teaching point is sound; the appeal to the specification is not.
findings.correction: A stronger argument is a balanced one: stereotypes also let audiences interpret media quickly, because a familiar shorthand communicates character or setting fast, and stereotypes can change over time as social attitudes shift.

findings.claim: Showing both sides of this argument, rather than a single-note complaint, is what examiners are looking for at the higher bands.
findings.problem: Unevidenced claim about examiner behaviour and band descriptors. The published assessment criteria for the 20-mark questions require analysis, judgements and conclusions; they do not specify that a two-sided treatment of stereotypes is required for the top bands.
findings.correction: Showing both sides of this argument, rather than a single-note complaint, produces the substantiated judgement the 20-mark questions ask for.

findings.claim: Time yourself against the marks: with 30 marks in each section, spend roughly 20 minutes on the 20-mark judgement question and 10 minutes on the 10-mark question, leaving time to plan before you write.
findings.problem: Misleading timing advice: this allocates only 60 minutes of writing across the whole paper, although the written examination for this component lasts 1 hour 30 minutes for 60 marks (roughly a minute and a half per mark). Students following it would leave about a third of the paper's time unused. The board does not publish a per-question timing.
findings.correction: Time yourself against the marks: the paper gives you about a minute and a half per mark, so allow roughly 30 minutes for each 20-mark judgement question and about 15 minutes for each 10-mark question, including a few minutes to plan before you write.

findings.claim: Linking them, rather than treating each in isolation, is what the higher-mark bands reward.
findings.problem: Unevidenced claim about band descriptors; the specification requires all four framework areas to be studied for Component 2 products but does not state that linking them is what the higher bands reward.
findings.correction: Linking them, rather than treating each in isolation, usually produces a stronger, better-supported argument.

findings.claim: Both set videos mix these modes, cutting between the artist performing and scenes that build a wider message about identity and self-worth.
findings.problem: This is inaccurate for Taylor Swift's "The Man" (2020), one of the two named set videos. The exam board's own published media factsheet on the set product states that because Swift is playing a character role she does not use direct mode of address, and that the video is mainly narrative-based, with only a short section at the end revealing the making of The Man. Telling students the video cuts between the artist performing to camera and narrative scenes would lead to a factually wrong media-language answer on the set product.
findings.correction: The two videos handle these modes differently. A body-positivity video can cut between performance-to-camera and narrative scenes, whereas "The Man" is mainly narrative-based: the artist plays a character rather than addressing the camera directly, and only the closing behind-the-scenes section reveals the performer beneath the prosthetics.

findings.claim: Both set videos combine performance mode and narrative mode, using visual codes such as costume, colour and editing rhythm to construct meaning beyond the song itself.
findings.problem: Same error repeated as a Key Fact students are told to memorise. Per the board's set-product factsheet for "The Man", the video is predominantly narrative with the artist in a character role and no direct mode of address, so it is not an example of performance mode combined with narrative mode.
findings.correction: Music videos draw on performance mode, narrative mode or a mix of both. Whichever video your class studied, identify which mode dominates — for example, a narrative-led video in which the artist plays a character rather than performing to camera — and explain how costume, colour and editing rhythm construct meaning beyond the song itself.

findings.claim: Name the two performance modes commonly combined in a contemporary music video.
findings.problem: Terminological error that contradicts the lesson's own glossary: performance mode and narrative mode are two distinct modes of music video, and narrative mode is not a type of performance mode. Students answering the question as worded would be describing something that does not exist.
findings.correction: Name the two modes commonly combined in a contemporary music video.

findings.claim: Simply spotting “there is a hero” earns little credit. Explaining that framing the artist as the hero of their own narrative reinforces a message of self-determination connects media language directly to representation — exactly the kind of link top-band answers make.
findings.problem: Unevidenced assertion about how work is credited and what reaches the top band. The specification and published assessment grids for this component are not quoted to this effect and no board document is cited.
findings.correction: Applying Proppian roles is only useful if it explains meaning. Explaining that framing the artist as the hero of their own narrative reinforces a message of self-determination connects media language directly to representation, which is the kind of developed analysis the assessment objectives require.

findings.claim: Applying this theory to the specific set video, rather than just naming the four needs, is what separates strong from weak answers.
findings.problem: Unevidenced claim about marking outcomes; no published board document states this.
findings.correction: Apply the theory to the specific set video rather than just naming the four needs, since the assessment objectives require application to the set product, not recall alone.

findings.claim: Linking a specific visual or narrative choice in the video to this wider context, rather than adding context as an afterthought, is exactly what the specification’s contexts strand rewards.
findings.problem: Unevidenced claim about what the specification rewards. The specification requires that contexts be studied in relation to the set products, but it does not state a reward criterion of this kind.
findings.correction: Link a specific visual or narrative choice in the video to this wider context, because contexts must be discussed in relation to the set product rather than added as a separate paragraph.

findings.claim: Q: "How many social or participatory media platforms must learners study alongside an artist's website?" A: "At least two."
findings.problem: A specific numerical study requirement is asserted as a specification rule. The specification's music section requires study of the artist's official website and their online, social and participatory media, but a minimum of two platforms could not be verified in any published board document; presenting an invented number as a requirement is a fabrication.
findings.correction: Q: "What must learners study alongside the music video itself in this topic?" A: "The artist's official website and their online, social and participatory media."

findings.claim: Learners study at least two social or participatory media platforms connected to the artist to understand how fans engage directly with, and sometimes help produce meaning around, the star image.
findings.problem: The 'at least two platforms' figure is not stated in the specification, which requires study of the artist's website and their online, social and participatory media without stipulating a number.
findings.correction: Learners also study the artist's online, social and participatory media to understand how fans engage directly with, and sometimes help produce meaning around, the star image.

findings.claim: Q: "What kind of funding model do contemporary commercial music videos typically rely on?" A: "Commercial funding, distributed across converging global platforms."
findings.problem: The answer largely restates the question ('commercial music videos' answered with 'commercial funding'), so the card tests nothing.
findings.correction: Q: "How is a contemporary music video normally paid for and made profitable?" A: "A record label funds it as promotion, recouping the cost through streaming, sales, advertising revenue and touring."

findings.claim: The video was made in partnership with the crowdfunding platform GoFundMe, using real footage of women who had run their own fundraising campaigns, an intertextual link between a music product and a charitable cause.
findings.problem: Fabricated partner and premise. The 'Intentions' video (released 7 February 2020, feat. Quavo) was made with Alexandria House, a Los Angeles non-profit providing transitional housing for women and children; the women featured are residents/graduates of Alexandria House speaking about homelessness, foster care and education, not people who ran crowdfunding campaigns. Bieber and Def Jam launched a $200,000 'Intentions Fund' to support them (Rolling Stone; Grammy.com). GoFundMe is not involved.
findings.correction: The video was made in partnership with Alexandria House, a Los Angeles non-profit that helps women and children move from crisis to stability. It features real residents and graduates of the project speaking about homelessness, foster care and education, and was released alongside a $200,000 'Intentions Fund' to support them — a link between a music product and a charitable cause.

findings.claim: Bieber’s Intentions constructs a representation of romantic devotion and generosity, reinforced by the real GoFundMe stories woven through the video.
findings.problem: Same fabricated detail: the real-life stories in the video come from women connected to the Alexandria House charity, not from GoFundMe campaigns (Rolling Stone; Grammy.com).
findings.correction: Bieber’s Intentions constructs a representation of romantic devotion and generosity, reinforced by the real stories of the Alexandria House residents woven through the video.

findings.claim: A fan engaging with Intentions and the GoFundMe stories might use it for social integration, feeling connected to a wider community of Bieber fans sharing and discussing the video online.
findings.problem: Repeats the fabricated GoFundMe attribution; the documentary inserts are the Alexandria House women's stories (Rolling Stone; Grammy.com).
findings.correction: A fan engaging with Intentions and the Alexandria House stories might use it for social integration, feeling connected to a wider community of Bieber fans sharing and discussing the video online.

findings.claim: Justin Bieber partnered with the platform _____ in the 'Intentions' video to highlight real stories of women running fundraising campaigns.
findings.problem: The correct-answer key ('GoFundMe') is factually wrong, and the premise is wrong: the partner was the charity Alexandria House and the women were residents rehoused by it, not fundraisers (Rolling Stone; Grammy.com). A student who learns this answer will write a fabricated industry detail in the exam.
findings.correction: Justin Bieber partnered with the Los Angeles charity _____ in the 'Intentions' video to highlight the real stories of women it had supported. Options: Alexandria House / Shelter / Comic Relief / Crisis — correct: Alexandria House.

findings.claim: {"q": "What organisation did Justin Bieber partner with for the 'Intentions' video?", "a": "GoFundMe."}
findings.problem: Wrong attribution: the partner organisation was Alexandria House, a non-profit providing housing and support for women and children in Los Angeles (Rolling Stone; Grammy.com).
findings.correction: {"q": "What organisation did Justin Bieber partner with for the 'Intentions' video?", "a": "Alexandria House, a Los Angeles non-profit supporting women and children."}

findings.claim: {"q": "What did the GoFundMe partnership in 'Intentions' highlight?", "a": "Real stories of women running fundraising campaigns."}
findings.problem: Both question and answer rest on the fabricated GoFundMe link; the video highlights the real experiences of women who had moved out of homelessness, foster care and domestic abuse via Alexandria House (Grammy.com; Rolling Stone).
findings.correction: {"q": "What did the Alexandria House partnership in 'Intentions' highlight?", "a": "The real experiences of women rebuilding their lives after homelessness and hardship."}

findings.claim: Mastering: Clearly explains the GoFundMe partnership and links it to a specific social context (e.g. growing use of artist platforms for socially responsible causes), with developed reasoning.
findings.problem: The indicative content rewards a fabricated detail. The 'Intentions' video's charitable partner was Alexandria House, with a $200,000 Intentions Fund (Rolling Stone; Grammy.com); no GoFundMe involvement is documented.
findings.correction: Mastering: Clearly explains the Alexandria House partnership and the Intentions Fund, and links these to a specific social context (e.g. growing use of artist platforms for socially responsible causes), with developed reasoning.

findings.claim: Examiners reward answers that move between these areas rather than treating each one in isolation.
findings.problem: Unevidenced claim about examiner behaviour. The assessment information for this component specifies which questions assess AO1 and which assess AO2; it does not state that marks are awarded for moving between framework areas.
findings.correction: Strong answers connect these areas rather than treating each one in isolation.

findings.claim: examiners' reports show that describing the product without reaching an argued position is the most common reason strong knowledge doesn't convert into top marks
findings.problem: Invented examiner-report claim. No published report is cited and none is quoted in the stated assessment information; only the requirement that higher-tariff analysis questions ask for judgements and conclusions can be supported.
findings.correction: For higher-tariff questions, always finish with a judgement or conclusion, because these questions explicitly ask you to make judgements and draw conclusions rather than only describe the product.

findings.claim: expect the kind of confident close camerawork, sharp editing paced to the track’s rhythm, and urban settings typical of British music videos, used to construct an image of pride and success rooted in a specific cultural scene
findings.problem: Misleading and hedged description of a set product students must analyse with specific detail. The board's own factsheet for this video describes it as celebrating the individuality of its characters and natural beauty, with the song's theme being ethnic empowerment — not generic 'urban settings typical of British music videos'. Writing about street/urban mise-en-scène that the video does not foreground would cost marks in a media language answer.
findings.correction: In Superheroes, Stormzy's grime and UK rap roots shape the visual style, but the video's focus is celebratory rather than street-based: it uses close, direct camerawork on a cast of Black British people of different ages, editing paced to the track, and costume and styling that celebrate individuality and natural beauty, constructing an image of pride, empowerment and success.

findings.claim: supporting a charitable message that resonated during a period of heightened attention to community support
findings.problem: Chronologically misleading: 'Intentions' and its video were released on 7 February 2020 (Wikipedia; Rolling Stone), before the pandemic period this phrasing implies. The relevant social context is celebrity philanthropy and artists using their platforms for social causes.
findings.correction: supporting a charitable message at a time when audiences increasingly expected major artists to use their platforms and profits for social causes

findings.claim: The specification allows schools to choose either Duran Duran’s “Rio” (1982) or TLC’s “Waterfalls” (1995) as the set music video from the past.
findings.problem: TLC's "Waterfalls" is not a set product for Component 2 Section B (Music) on this specification, and no such either/or choice of past video is offered. Eduqas support material lists the Component 2 music video set products as the contemporary artists (Stormzy / Lizzo / Taylor Swift) plus the historical video from the 1980s/early 1990s, Duran Duran's "Rio" (1982) — the Eduqas resources page refers to factsheets for "the set music videos from the 1980s and early 1990s", and Eduqas-aligned teaching bundles cover exactly three Component 2 music video set texts (Taylor Swift, Stormzy, Duran Duran). Presenting "Waterfalls" as an examinable option sends students to revise a product they will not be assessed on.
findings.correction: The set music video from the past for this unit is Duran Duran’s “Rio” (1982). Check with your teacher which contemporary videos your class studied alongside it, but “Rio” is the past video you will be examined on.

findings.claim: You will study either Duran Duran’s “Rio” (1982) or TLC’s “Waterfalls” (1995). Both are famous videos from their decades, but they construct very different meanings through very different choices of media language.
findings.problem: Out of scope: "Waterfalls" (1995) is not on this board's music set product list for this unit; the historical music video studied is Duran Duran's "Rio" (1982). A 1995 video also falls outside the spec's "1980s and early 1990s" historical category.
findings.correction: You will study Duran Duran’s “Rio” (1982) as the music video from the past, alongside your two contemporary set videos. Comparing it with the contemporary videos shows how the pop music video constructs meaning differently in different eras.

findings.claim: The set past music videos are Duran Duran’s “Rio” (1982) and TLC’s “Waterfalls” (1995). “Rio” constructs glamour and escapism; “Waterfalls” constructs a cautionary narrative about real social issues.
findings.problem: Invented set product presented as a Key Fact. Only "Rio" (1982) is a set music video from the past on this specification; "Waterfalls" is not a set product, so this Key Fact would be memorised as false examinable knowledge.
findings.correction: The set music video from the past is Duran Duran’s “Rio” (1982). It constructs glamour, escapism and exoticism through its mise-en-scène of yacht, tropical location and high fashion.

findings.claim: TLC, Waterfalls (1995): Media Language and Narrative … Representation and Context in Waterfalls … Comparing Rio and Waterfalls Across Time
findings.problem: Two whole teaching sections, a Key Fact and a collapsible activity are devoted to a product that is not a set product for this board and unit. The factual content about the video is accurate, but teaching it as assessed material diverts revision time from the actual set products (the two contemporary videos and their online presence, plus "Rio").
findings.correction: Delete the "Waterfalls" sections and replace them with comparison of "Rio" against the two contemporary set music videos your class studied, covering media language, representation and relevant contexts.

findings.claim: is built around a luxury yacht and exotic coastal locations filmed in Sri Lanka and Antigua
findings.problem: Wrong location detail. The "Rio" video was shot in Antigua (with additional studio/beach work); Sri Lanka was the location for other Duran Duran videos from the same period, including "Hungry Like the Wolf", "Save a Prayer" and "Lonely in Your Nightmare". Students quoting Sri Lanka as a "Rio" location in a context answer would be giving an inaccurate example.
findings.correction: is built around a luxury yacht and exotic coastal locations filmed in Antigua in the Caribbean (the band shot other videos of the same period in Sri Lanka)

findings.claim: The past video is studied for three areas of the theoretical framework: media language, representation and media contexts.
findings.problem: Misstates the specification. The theoretical framework has four areas — media language, representation, media industries and audiences — and contexts are not one of them. The specification's guidance is that the historical music video in Component 2 Section B is studied only in relation to media language and representation (with reference to relevant contexts, which are studied alongside the framework, not as part of it).
findings.correction: The past video is studied for two areas of the theoretical framework — media language and representation — and in relation to relevant social, cultural and historical contexts.

findings.claim: This paper’s Music questions reward synoptic thinking — connecting media language, representation and context rather than treating them separately.
findings.problem: Unevidenced claim about what the exam rewards; the specification does not state that Music questions reward "synoptic thinking". What it does state is that reference to relevant contexts may be required and that the historical video is assessed on media language and representation.
findings.correction: Music questions on the past video focus on media language and representation, and may require you to refer to relevant contexts. Be ready to explain not just what you see on screen, but why the producers made those choices given the historical moment the video was made in.

findings.claim: A balanced answer also recognises the specification’s point that stereotypes are not only negative — they let audiences read meaning quickly.
findings.problem: Attributes to the specification a statement it does not make. The point about stereotypes functioning as a quick shorthand is a standard critical observation, not a specification claim.
findings.correction: A balanced answer also recognises that stereotypes are not only negative — they let audiences read meaning quickly.

findings.claim: Which media language technique dominates the visual style of TLC's "Waterfalls" video? / TLC's "Waterfalls" uses a _____ narrative structure to address serious social issues such as HIV/AIDS and gang violence.
findings.problem: Both checks test a product that is not a set product for this board and unit, so correct answers carry no exam value.
findings.correction: Replace with checks on the set products, e.g. MCQ: "Which setting dominates the mise-en-scène of Duran Duran's 'Rio'?" (options: a luxury yacht in a tropical location / a derelict warehouse / a city nightclub / a recording studio; correct: 0) and fill: "MTV launched in _____, creating industry pressure for visually spectacular music videos." (options: 1981 / 1975 / 1987 / 1991; correct: 0).

findings.claim: {"q": "When was TLC's \"Waterfalls\" released?", "a": "1995."} and the cards on its director, water effect and two narrative strands
findings.problem: Five of the twelve cards drill detail on "Waterfalls", which is not a set product for this board and unit; the facts are correct but unexaminable.
findings.correction: Replace with cards on the set products, e.g. {"q": "Which Caribbean island was Duran Duran's 'Rio' video filmed on?", "a": "Antigua."}; {"q": "Why did record labels want visually spectacular videos in the early 1980s?", "a": "MTV had launched in 1981, so eye-catching videos were needed to promote singles on the new music channel."}; {"q": "How does the mise-en-scène of 'Rio' construct escapism?", "a": "Yacht, tropical sea and bright sunshine connote wealth and a world away from 1980s Britain."}

findings.claim: Identify the visual effect used throughout TLC's music video for "Waterfalls" to represent the song's central lyric metaphor. / Explain briefly how TLC's "Waterfalls" uses narrative to address a serious social issue. / Analyse how media language is used in TLC's "Waterfalls" to construct meanings about risk and consequence.
findings.problem: Three of the six practice questions are set on a product that is not on this board's music set product list, so they cannot resemble a real exam question for this unit.
findings.correction: Re-set these on the set products, e.g. 1 mark: "Identify one item of costume in Duran Duran's 'Rio' that connotes wealth."; 3 marks: "Explain briefly how editing in 'Rio' constructs a sense of energy and spectacle."; 15 marks: "Analyse how media language is used in Duran Duran's 'Rio' to construct meanings of glamour and escapism." (mark guidance as written, with the examples changed to yacht, tropical location, costume, fast cutting and performance footage).

findings.claim: If you studied Stormzy’s Superheroes or Justin Bieber’s Intentions, the paired website is stormzy.com or justinbiebermusic.com.
findings.problem: Justin Bieber's 'Intentions' (and justinbiebermusic.com) is not an Eduqas GCSE Media Studies Component 2 Section B music set product. The board's own documentation identifies the contemporary music video and online set products as Stormzy, Lizzo and Taylor Swift only (Eduqas Media Studies bulletin, Sept 2024: new GCSE resources 'for Stormzy, Lizzo, and Taylor Swift'; the GCSE specification's content advisory note refers to 'Good as Hell and Superheroes'). Teaching an invented set product as assessed material wastes revision time and misdirects preparation.
findings.correction: If you studied Stormzy’s Superheroes, the paired website is stormzy.com. The contemporary music set products are Lizzo’s Good as Hell, Stormzy’s Superheroes and Taylor Swift’s The Man, each studied with the artist’s official website — check which of these your class has been set.

findings.claim: {"q": "Which website is Justin Bieber's website, set as an alternative to Stormzy's?", "a": "justinbiebermusic.com"}
findings.problem: Justin Bieber is not one of the board's music set products for this unit, so the card teaches a non-existent set product; the 'alternative to Stormzy's' pairing is also invented, as the contemporary options are Lizzo, Stormzy and Taylor Swift rather than fixed pairs.
findings.correction: {"q": "Which three contemporary artists' music videos and websites are set for study?", "a": "Lizzo, Stormzy and Taylor Swift."}

findings.claim: You are required to study at least two social and participatory platforms alongside the website, since the specification no longer names specific platforms — be ready to discuss whichever ones your set artist actually uses.
findings.problem: The specification sets no minimum number of social and participatory media platforms. It requires study of the artist's online presence — the website (home page design, links to other content, interactive links) and the associated social and participatory media — without stipulating 'at least two' platforms. This is an invented requirement presented as a specification rule.
findings.correction: Alongside the website you also study the social and participatory media the artist uses — the specification does not name particular platforms, so be ready to discuss whichever ones your set artist actually uses.

findings.claim: {"q": "How many social and participatory media platforms must learners study?", "a": "At least two."}
findings.problem: No such minimum exists in the specification; the requirement is to study the artist's website and its associated social and participatory media, with no stated number of platforms.
findings.correction: {"q": "Which social and participatory media must learners study for the music option?", "a": "Those used by the set artist alongside their official website; no specific platforms are named."}

findings.claim: since generic recall without application won’t reach the higher bands
findings.problem: Unevidenced claim about marking and band placement. The specification and published assessment materials do not state that theory recall without application blocks the higher bands for this component; GCSE mark bands reward accurate, developed and well-exemplified explanation generally.
findings.correction: since answers that apply ideas about audience needs to the specific website or platform are fuller and better supported than answers that only define the idea.

findings.claim: Uses and Gratifications theory must be applied to a specific need a website or platform satisfies, not just recalled as a list.
findings.problem: The GCSE specification does not name academic theorists or require any named theory (named theories are an A Level requirement); stating that Uses and Gratifications 'must' be applied presents an optional teaching tool as a specification requirement.
findings.correction: Ideas about audience needs (such as Blumler and Katz's uses and gratifications) are most useful when applied to a specific need a website or platform satisfies, rather than recalled as a list.

findings.claim: This links directly to how people’s media practices connect to their sense of actual and desired self — who they are, and who they want to be seen as.
findings.problem: The phrase 'actual and desired self' is not specification wording for this GCSE; the specification frames audience use in terms of identity, needs and how audiences interpret and use media. Presenting borrowed phrasing as specification language risks students using terminology the mark scheme does not recognise.
findings.correction: This links to how audiences use media as part of their sense of identity — aligning themselves with an artist's image to express who they are, or who they want to be seen as.

findings.claim: Questions on The Sun always use command words like ‘explain’ or ‘analyse’ applied to industry or audience issues
findings.problem: This is an invented claim about question format that the specification does not make, and it contradicts the board's own registered tariffs for this qualification, which include 1-mark Name/Identify and 2-mark State with Detail items — as the lesson's own practice questions demonstrate ('Name the organisation that regulates The Sun...'). The specification states only that the focus of Section B is on the set products as examples of media industries and audiences, not which command words will be used.
findings.correction: Questions in this topic focus on industry and audience issues rather than on the newspaper’s design or language, and they range from short identification and short-explanation questions up to extended responses.

findings.claim: A common mistake is naming Blumler and Katz’s theory without applying it to a Sun example; examiners reward the application, not the recall.
findings.problem: Unevidenced assertion about examiner behaviour and about what most candidates get wrong; no published board document for this qualification states this. Assertions about what examiners reward or penalise should not be presented as fact.
findings.correction: Always apply Blumler and Katz’s theory to a specific example from The Sun rather than simply naming the theory — the specification requires you to use theories to explain how audiences respond to the set product.

findings.claim: For this topic you study one complete print edition alongside selected pages of the website, including the homepage and at least one other page, so you can see how the same brand is presented differently across platforms.
findings.problem: Invented study requirement. The specification does not prescribe 'the homepage and at least one other page'; it says only that learners study the set product as an example of industry and audience issues and that the product's online presence is a key way into those issues. The board's own FAQ confirms centres choose which edition to study.
findings.correction: For this topic you study a complete edition of the newspaper together with its online presence, including the thesun.co.uk website, so you can see how the same brand is presented across platforms.

findings.claim: The theory only earns marks when it is applied like this to the actual set product, not simply listed.
findings.problem: A claim about mark-scheme behaviour that the specification does not make. The specification requires the use of relevant theories to understand audiences; it does not state that naming a theory earns zero marks.
findings.correction: The theory is most useful when applied like this to the set product, with a specific example, rather than simply listed by name.

findings.claim: Here, examiners are not testing your ability to describe The Sun’s masthead, headline style or photography.
findings.problem: The substance is correct (the specification states that for this section learners should not engage in analysis of the textual features of the set products) but the claim is framed as unevidenced examiner behaviour, and the same newspaper is also a set product elsewhere in the paper where media language analysis is exactly what is assessed. Note also the flat 'earns no credit' phrasing in the following Key Fact.
findings.correction: Here the requirement is different: the exam board states that for this section you should not analyse the textual features of the set product, but study it as an example of industry and audience issues. (Amend the Key Fact to: 'Focus on ownership, funding, regulation, targeting and audience theory rather than on colours, headlines or photography, which belong to the media language and representation topic.')

findings.claim: it makes its money mainly from advertising and from sales of the newspaper and its digital content
findings.problem: Slight imprecision: The Sun removed its digital paywall in 2015, so its online revenue is predominantly advertising (plus related commercial ventures) rather than sales of digital content; the same wording appears in the 2-mark mark scheme ('cover-price/digital sales').
findings.correction: it makes its money mainly from advertising — in print and online — and from cover-price sales of the printed newspaper

findings.claim: Examiners give no credit for detailed textual analysis of this set product — the focus must stay on industry and audience issues.
findings.problem: Unevidenced claim about examiner behaviour/marking. The specification and Guidance for Teaching state only that the framework is divided by section ("media language and representation in Section A; media industries and audiences in Section B" — Eduqas GCSE Media Studies Guidance for Teaching); no board document says references to the programme's content earn no credit, and a candidate may legitimately use programme detail to support an audience-appeal point.
findings.correction: In this section of the specification the assessment focuses on media industries and audiences, so your answers should be built around production, funding, regulation, distribution and audience issues rather than detailed analysis of sound or presentation style.

findings.claim: Desert Island Discs is studied only as an example of radio industry and audience issues. Textual analysis of its sound, structure or presentation style earns no credit — the focus is on production, funding, regulation and how audiences use the programme.
findings.problem: "Earns no credit" is a claim about marks that the specification does not make; the spec allocates industries and audiences to this section but does not state that any reference to the programme's content is unrewarded. Presenting an invented marking rule as a memorised Key Fact is misleading.
findings.correction: Desert Island Discs is studied for radio industry and audience issues: production, funding, regulation, distribution and how audiences use the programme. Keep answers focused on these areas rather than on analysing sound or presentation style.

findings.claim: The highest-scoring answers apply these needs specifically to the programme rather than simply listing the theory.
findings.problem: Unevidenced assertion about examiner expectations/what scores highest; no published board document for this unit is quoted in support.
findings.correction: Aim to apply each named need to the programme itself with specific examples, rather than only describing the theory in general terms.

findings.claim: Do not drift into describing the sound of the programme or a specific episode’s content in detail; that kind of textual observation earns no marks here.
findings.problem: Another invented mark claim about examiner behaviour; the specification does not state that episode detail scores zero in this section, and episode detail can legitimately support an industry or audience point.
findings.correction: Do not drift into extended description of the sound of the programme or of one episode; use episode detail only briefly, and only where it supports an industry or audience point.

findings.claim: audiences increasingly listen on demand rather than tuning in live, a trend called <dfn class="term" ...>convergence</dfn>
findings.problem: Terminology error that conflicts with the lesson's own (correct) glossary definition. Convergence is the coming together of previously separate technologies and platforms; the move from live listening to on-demand listening is a change in audience consumption (and audience fragmentation), not convergence itself.
findings.correction: audiences increasingly listen on demand rather than tuning in live — a change in consumption habits that the industry meets through <dfn class="term" data-def="The coming together of previously separate media technologies and platforms, such as radio content becoming available as an on-demand podcast.">convergence</dfn>, as the same content is delivered across radio, online and podcast platforms

findings.claim: {"q": "Name two platforms Desert Island Discs is distributed on besides live radio.", "a": "BBC Sounds and podcast."}
findings.problem: Breach of flashcard rules: the answer is a list of items, which should be split into separate cards.
findings.correction: {"q": "On which BBC on-demand service can listeners stream Desert Island Discs?", "a": "BBC Sounds."} and a second card: {"q": "In what downloadable audio format is Desert Island Discs also distributed?", "a": "As a podcast."}

findings.claim: plus key pages from its website, including the homepage and at least one other page
findings.problem: Over-specified study requirement. The specification requires study of one complete episode and the programme's website; it does not stipulate a homepage plus a minimum number of additional pages (that phrasing belongs to online/social media products elsewhere in the course).
findings.correction: plus the programme’s website

findings.claim: Desert Island Discs sits within the <dfn class="term" ...>talk radio</dfn> genre — programming built around conversation rather than continuous music.
findings.problem: Slight imprecision: the programme is a speech/music hybrid — the castaway chooses eight musical tracks that are played as an integral part of the format, as the board's own set product factsheet material and BBC descriptions make clear.
findings.correction: Desert Island Discs sits within the <dfn class="term" data-def="A radio genre built around spoken conversation, interview or discussion rather than continuous music programming.">talk radio</dfn> genre, though it is a hybrid form: extended interview and biography built around the guest’s eight chosen music tracks, rather than continuous music programming.

findings.claim: No Time to Die is studied for media industries only. You will not be asked to analyse its media language or its audience appeal — only how it was produced, owned, funded, marketed and regulated.
findings.problem: Over-extended and mark-affecting. The specification restricts the FILM to media industries in the Exploring Media Industries and Audiences section, but the No Time to Die (2021) film poster is a set product in Component 1 Section A (Exploring Media Language and Representation), alongside The Man with the Golden Gun (1974), and IS assessed for media language and representation (WJEC/Eduqas set product factsheet 'No Time to Die (2021) – poster and film industry'; Component 1 Section A set product list for 2027). Telling students they will never face a media language question on No Time to Die could make them skip a Section A poster analysis worth up to 15 marks.
findings.correction: In the industries and audiences section, No Time to Die is studied for media industries only — how it was produced, owned, funded, marketed and regulated. You will not be asked audience questions on the film here, and you never analyse the moving image (camerawork, editing, sound, performance). Remember, though, that the No Time to Die film poster is a separate set product for media language and representation in the first section of the paper.

findings.claim: No Time to Die is studied only for media industries, using the 007.com website as evidence — never analyse its media language.
findings.problem: Same error as the Key Fact. The film is industries-only in the industries and audiences section, but the No Time to Die film poster is a Component 1 Section A set product assessed for media language and representation, so 'never analyse its media language' is false for the paper as a whole.
findings.correction: In the industries and audiences section, No Time to Die is studied for media industries only, using the 007.com website as evidence — keep media language analysis for the film poster, which is a separate set product in the first section of the paper.

findings.claim: Which of the following is the correct focus for studying No Time to Die on the exam? / Media industries only
findings.problem: As worded ('on the exam'), the keyed answer is wrong: the No Time to Die film poster is a Component 1 Section A set product studied for media language and representation, while the film itself is industries-only in Section B. The question needs restricting to the industries and audiences section.
findings.correction: Change the stem to: 'In the industries and audiences section of the paper, what is the correct focus for studying the film No Time to Die?' (correct option remains 'Media industries only').

findings.claim: {"q": "What must you NOT do when answering an exam question on No Time to Die?", "a": "Analyse its media language or textual features."}
findings.problem: Factually wrong as an unqualified rule: the No Time to Die poster is a set product for media language and representation in Component 1 Section A, so media language analysis is required there. The restriction applies only to the film in the industries and audiences section.
findings.correction: {"q": "In an industries question on the film No Time to Die, what must you avoid doing?", "a": "Describing the film's shots, sound or performances instead of industry points such as ownership, funding or regulation."}

findings.claim: Never drift into describing shots, dialogue or performances from the film itself; that earns zero credit here.
findings.problem: Unevidenced claim about marking. The specification states only that extracts from the film must be used to illustrate industry points; it does not state that textual reference 'earns zero credit', and no published mark scheme statement to that effect was found. It also risks reinforcing the mistaken idea that media language is never assessed on this set product (the poster is a Section A product).
findings.correction: Keep any reference to the film tied to an industry point — an industries question rewards concepts such as ownership, funding, convergence and regulation, not description of shots, dialogue or performances.

findings.claim: You are not asked to analyse Fortnite’s textual features — there is no marking credit for describing gameplay, colour schemes or camera angles.
findings.problem: Overstates a mark claim the specification does not make. The Eduqas GCSE Media Studies specification states only that for Section B "learners should not engage in analysis of the textual features of the set products, but should study them as examples of the relevant industry and audience issues"; it makes no statement about credit being withheld. The Eduqas GCSE Examiners' Report (Summer 2024) records that candidates who used textual features of the Fortnite website (colour, imagery, intertextuality) to explain how it engaged users were "able to reach the highest bands", so a blanket 'no marking credit' claim is misleading.
findings.correction: You are not asked to analyse Fortnite as a text in this section. The exam board states that learners should not analyse the textual features of Section B set products, but should study them as examples of industry and audience issues, so answers must be built around industry and audience points rather than description of gameplay.

findings.claim: Analysing its visual style, camerawork or mise-en-scène earns no credit — examiners want industry and audience knowledge applied to this named product.
findings.problem: Unevidenced claim about examiner behaviour and about credit. No published exam board document states that examiners 'want' this or that such material 'earns no credit'; the specification only defines the focus of study for Section B.
findings.correction: Fortnite is studied for media industries and audiences only. The exam board's focus for this section is industry and audience issues, so answers should apply that knowledge to Fortnite rather than analyse its visual style, camerawork or mise-en-scène.

findings.claim: Naming the theory alone earns little credit — the higher marks come from applying each need directly to how Fortnite specifically satisfies it.
findings.problem: Invented claim about mark allocation and examiner expectation. No exam board document quoted in the scope for this unit states how marks are split between naming and applying a theory; the specification says only that learners will develop the ability to use relevant theories or theoretical perspectives appropriately.
findings.correction: A strong answer does more than name the theory: it applies each need directly to how Fortnite specifically satisfies it, using precise detail from the product.

findings.claim: The Fortnite website and in-game menus categorise players by activity — competitive modes for skilled players, creative modes for younger or casual players — showing how organisations segment a mass audience into smaller groups with different needs.
findings.problem: Mischaracterises the set product. Fortnite Creative is a build/user-generated-content sandbox in which players design and publish their own islands (alongside Battle Royale and Save the World); it is not a mode aimed at 'younger or casual players', and competitive play is not restricted to 'skilled players'. A student repeating this in an exam would be describing the product inaccurately.
findings.correction: The Fortnite website and in-game menus categorise players by the type of experience they want — battle royale matches, competitive and tournament play, and Creative mode, where players build and share their own islands — showing how organisations segment a mass audience into smaller groups with different needs.

findings.claim: {"q": "What does it mean to say Fortnite audiences are 'active' rather than 'passive'?", "a": "They livestream, create fan content and follow esports."}
findings.problem: Breaches the flashcard rule that an answer must not be a list of items ('X, Y and Z') — each example belongs on its own card.
findings.correction: {"q": "What does it mean to say Fortnite audiences are 'active' rather than 'passive'?", "a": "They respond to and create content around the game instead of simply consuming it."}

findings.claim: Compare how the set Vogue and GQ front covers use media language and representation to construct meanings for their target audiences." / "25 marks — Compare with Unseen Resource
findings.problem: The 25-mark question on this board is not a comparison of two set products. The specification states that Component 1 Question 2 part (b) (25 marks) "will require a comparison of an unseen resource with a set product in the same media form" (Eduqas GCSE Media Studies specification, Component 1 Section A). A practice question asking students to compare the two set magazine covers with each other misrepresents the task they will actually meet, and the mark guidance repeats the error ("reference to both covers", "each cover").
findings.correction: Question: "Compare the set Vogue front cover with the unseen magazine front cover provided in the resource booklet. How do they use media language and representation to construct meanings for their target audiences?" Mark guidance: "Mastering: sustained, well-substantiated comparison of the set product and the unseen resource running through every point, addressing both media language and representation with sophisticated terminology and a clear line of argument. Secure: clear comparison with relevant points on both media language and representation, supported with reference to both the set product and the unseen resource. Developing: some comparative points but treatment may be unbalanced or descriptive rather than analytical. Emerging: separate description of the set product and the unseen resource with little or no genuine comparison."

findings.claim: Examiners reward explanation of the meanings those features construct and why a producer chose them.
findings.problem: Unevidenced assertion about examiner behaviour. No published assessment material for this component is quoted or provided that states what examiners reward; the assessment objectives should be described in terms of what the question requires, not what examiners are said to want.
findings.correction: Marks for media language analysis are given for explaining the meanings those features construct and why a producer might have chosen them, not for identifying features alone.

findings.claim: This is why analysing image and cover line together, rather than separately, earns higher marks: the two elements are designed to work as a combined system.
findings.problem: Unevidenced claim about how marks are awarded; no assessment rule or published mark scheme is provided that states integrated image/text analysis is credited more highly than separate analysis.
findings.correction: This is why it is more effective to analyse image and cover line together rather than separately: the two elements are designed to work as a combined system.

findings.claim: 1 mark for correctly identifying 'masthead'. No credit for 'title' or 'logo' alone without the specific term.
findings.problem: The second sentence invents a marking rule that no published mark scheme for this component states. Guidance should describe the creditworthy answer, not assert refusals of credit that the specification and mark schemes do not make.
findings.correction: 1 mark for correctly identifying 'masthead'. The specific media terminology is required.

findings.claim: The 1974 poster surrounds Bond with decorative, sexualised female figures; the 2021 poster instead reflects the franchise’s move toward more diverse and less objectified representations, including the new 007, Nomi.
findings.problem: Placed in a Key Fact about the two posters (and paired with the revision prompt 'list two differences between how the 1974 and 2021 Bond posters represent gender'), this implies Nomi appears on the No Time to Die poster. The set-product No Time to Die theatrical poster foregrounds Daniel Craig's Bond alone; Nomi's 007 status is a feature of the film's narrative and wider campaign, not of the poster image itself. A student citing 'Nomi on the poster' as poster evidence in a media language/representation answer would be describing something not in the set product.
findings.correction: The 1974 poster surrounds Bond with decorative, sexualised female figures; the 2021 poster drops this convention entirely, showing Bond alone in a restrained, serious composition. The franchise's wider move toward more diverse representation is seen in the film itself, where Lashana Lynch's Nomi holds the 007 designation.

findings.claim: The poster makes extensive use of Roger Moore’s established star image as a smooth, unflappable Bond, positioning him centrally and confidently.
findings.problem: Imprecise: The Man with the Golden Gun (1974) was only Moore's second appearance as Bond, after Live and Let Die (1973), so his 'Bond' star image was barely established in 1974. His recognisable smooth, unflappable persona came primarily from television roles such as The Saint and The Persuaders!, which is what the 1974 marketing traded on.
findings.correction: The poster makes extensive use of Roger Moore's star image — the suave, unflappable persona built up in television series such as The Saint and carried into his second Bond film — positioning him centrally and confidently.

findings.claim: When answering the extended comparison question, examiners want to see continuous comparison, not two separate mini-essays.
findings.problem: Unevidenced claim about examiner preferences. No published specification or assessment guidance for this component states what examiners 'want' in this way; the mark-affecting requirement is what the assessment criteria reward, not an asserted examiner preference.
findings.correction: When answering the extended comparison question, aim for continuous comparison rather than two separate mini-essays.

findings.claim: The Guardian follows conventions associated with the broadsheet tradition
findings.problem: Potentially misleading about the set product itself: The Guardian has not been printed at broadsheet size since 2005 (Berliner) and has been printed in tabloid/compact format since 15 January 2018 (Design Week; Britannica), so the set 18 January 2022 edition is physically tabloid-sized even though its content style is 'quality press'. A student writing that the set Guardian front page 'is a broadsheet' in size would be factually wrong about the product in front of them.
findings.correction: The Guardian is a quality-press ('broadsheet-style') paper, although since 2018 it has actually been printed in a tabloid/compact page size, so the set 18 January 2022 edition is small-format. It follows conventions associated with the quality-press tradition: a denser text-to-image ratio, more formal headline language, and a layout that assumes the reader will spend longer reading.

findings.claim: Secure: Both named with a minor spelling error.
findings.problem: Makes accuracy of spelling a mark-affecting criterion. No marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar are awarded for this component in the stated assessment rules, and a one-mark 'Name/Identify' response should be credited if the paper is identifiable.
findings.correction: Mastering: Both papers correctly named (The Guardian and The Sun). Secure: Both papers identified, though one is named imprecisely. Developing: Only one paper correctly named. Emerging: No correct paper named.

findings.claim: (parse failure)
findings.problem: Expecting ',' delimiter: line 1 column 3009 (char 3008)

findings.claim: A 1956 advertisement was produced for readers of mainstream print magazines with no television advertising to compete against, so illustration and lengthy body copy could hold attention.
findings.problem: Factually wrong historical context. Commercial television advertising began in Britain on ITV on 22 September 1955 (the first UK TV advert was for Gibbs SR toothpaste), and by 1956 ITV had rolled out to the Midlands and the North. A 1956 print advertisement was therefore competing with television advertising. Students who repeat this in a 5-mark context question or the context part of the comparison question would be writing an inaccurate contextual claim.
findings.correction: A 1956 advertisement was produced for readers of mainstream print magazines at a time when commercial television advertising was still brand new in Britain — ITV had only begun carrying adverts in September 1955 — so print remained a dominant advertising medium and illustration with lengthy body copy could still hold a reader’s attention.

findings.claim: Examiners reward a genuinely comparative response, so use connectives such as “whereas”, “similarly” and “in contrast” throughout
findings.problem: Unevidenced claim about examiner behaviour. The specification states only that the question assesses representation in relation to one set product and one unseen resource in the same media form; it does not say what examiners 'reward'. The requirement should be stated as a requirement of the question, not as an assertion about examiners.
findings.correction: The comparison question requires you to compare the set product with the unseen resource, so a response that deals with each text in isolation will not meet the demands of the question; use connectives such as “whereas”, “similarly” and “in contrast” throughout

findings.claim: Quality Street’s 1956 advertisement was produced in a period of post-war British recovery, shortly after rationing on sweets had ended.
findings.problem: Imprecise dating. Sweet rationing in Britain ended on 5 February 1953 and all food rationing ended in July 1954 — about three years before the 1956 advertisement, so 'shortly after' overstates the proximity. Naming the date is more useful for a context question.
findings.correction: Quality Street’s 1956 advertisement was produced in a period of post-war British recovery, a few years after sweet rationing ended in 1953 and all food rationing ended in 1954.

findings.claim: Quality Street (1956) is a magazine advertisement for a boxed chocolate assortment
findings.problem: Minor product inaccuracy: Quality Street (launched by Mackintosh’s in 1936) is a boxed/tinned assortment of toffees and sweets as well as chocolates, not a chocolate-only assortment.
findings.correction: Quality Street (1956) is a magazine advertisement for a boxed assortment of chocolates and toffees

findings.claim: Both episodes were made for commercially funded television, meaning the broadcaster generates revenue through advertising and subscription rather than direct government funding.
findings.problem: Inaccurate industry detail. ITV's core funding is advertising and sponsorship, not subscription — ITV1 and the standard ITVX tier are free to view and advertising-funded (only the optional ITVX Premium tier is subscription-based). The contrast normally drawn with public service broadcasters such as the BBC is the licence fee, which is not 'government funding'. The Eduqas specification frames the television crime drama products in terms of approaches to public service broadcasting and commercial funding, so this could mislead in an 'industries' answer.
findings.correction: Both episodes were made for a commercially funded broadcaster: ITV is a commercial public service broadcaster that generates its revenue mainly from advertising and sponsorship, rather than from the licence fee that funds the BBC.

findings.claim: Applying this theory to a specific moment in either episode — rather than just naming it — is what earns higher marks.
findings.problem: Unevidenced claim about how marks are awarded. The Eduqas GCSE Media Studies specification and its assessment grids do not state that naming versus applying a named theory determines the mark band; named theorists are not a requirement of the GCSE theoretical framework at all.
findings.correction: Using a theory is only useful if you link it to a specific moment in the episode, so that your point is supported by evidence from the product rather than left as a general statement.

findings.claim: For the television crime drama option, you study two contrasting episodes using all four areas of the theoretical framework: media language, representation, media industries and audiences.
findings.problem: Incomplete against the specification's in-depth study requirement, which covers the four framework areas together with media contexts — and the lesson itself goes on to teach a 'Media Contexts' section.
findings.correction: For the television crime drama option, you study two contrasting episodes using all four areas of the theoretical framework — media language, representation, media industries and audiences — together with the relevant media contexts.

findings.claim: Trigger Point (2024) and The Sweeney (1975) are studied across all four framework areas: media language, representation, industries and audiences.

findings.correction: From 2027 the set television products are Trigger Point, Man Like Mobeen (Series 1, 2017, BBC Three) and Modern Family (Series 8, Episode 2, “A Stereotypical Day”, 2016, ABC). Your centre chooses one of these to study and the exam extract will be taken from that product.

findings.problem: Fabricated attribution to the specification: Friends is not a set product in this specification at all, so the specification makes no such statement about it.

findings.problem: Wrong year for Man Like Mobeen (Series 1 premiered 17 December 2017) and Friends is not a set product; the unit requires in-depth study of one set television product, not a paired comparison.

Friends is also not a set product.
findings.correction: When you tackle the extract-based question on your set television product, remember it comes in two parts: part (a) asks you to analyse media language or representation in the extract, and part (b) asks you to analyse and reach judgements or conclusions.

(The part (a) / part (b) split and the focus of the second question are as stated in the specification and are correct.)

Instead, explain what specific choices of camera, editing or dialogue construct, and reach a conclusion about the meanings or representations they create. For the second question, on media industries and audiences, always tie your point directly to Modern Family rather than writing generally about sitcoms.

Secure: Explains the broadcasting and streaming arrangements with relevant industry terminology. Developing: Identifies relevant distributors but explanation of industry significance is limited. Emerging: Names one or more broadcasters with little explanation.

(ABC); 'Modern Family's set episode is Season 8, Episode _____' (2); and a matching item pairing Modern Family with 'plays on stereotypes of age, gender and ethnicity' and Man Like Mobeen with 'a British production made for BBC Three'.
