findings.claim: You will not know in advance which extract will be set, so you must be equally prepared to analyse any of them using the same framework.
findings.problem: This misdescribes the paper. The specification states that one extract is set from each set television programme — Trigger Point (from 2027 onwards), Man Like Mobeen and Modern Family — "to be screened as appropriate by the centre". Centres study one set option/programme and the centre screens the extract for the programme studied, so candidates know which programme their extract comes from (it is taken from the set episode they have studied); only the particular three minutes is unseen. Telling students to prepare all three programmes sends them to revise material they will not be assessed on.
findings.correction: The extract is taken from the set television programme your class has studied — the exam board sets one extract for each set programme and your centre screens the one that matches your option. You know the programme and the set episode in advance; what you do not know is which three minutes of it will be shown, so you must be able to apply the framework to any moment of that episode.

findings.claim: With 30 marks available and roughly 30 minutes of exam time, allocate your time proportionally: about 20 minutes for Question 1 and 10 minutes for Question 2.
findings.problem: Invented timing. The specification sets the component as a single written examination covering both the television section and the music section and states only the viewing arrangements (two minutes' reading time, a three-minute extract played twice with a six-minute note-taking break); it gives no recommended minutes for the television section and no per-question time split. The past paper simply tells candidates to use "the remaining examination time to complete both sections". A fabricated 30-minute allocation also understates the time actually available for the 30 marks in this section.
findings.correction: Question 1 is worth 20 marks and Question 2 is worth 10 marks, so give roughly twice as much of your writing time to Question 1 as to Question 2. Remember that the reading time, the two viewings and the six-minute note-taking break all come out of the total examination time, and that you must leave time for the other section of the paper. Spend the first minute of Question 1 planning a brief structure before you start writing.

findings.claim: {"q": "How should the 30 exam minutes be split between Question 1 and Question 2?", "a": "About 20 minutes for Question 1, 10 for Question 2."}
findings.problem: The card rests on a timing the specification does not state: there is no published 30-minute allocation for the television section and no per-question timing. The exam board specifies only the reading time, extract length, number of viewings and note-taking break.
findings.correction: {"q": "How should writing time be divided between Question 1 and Question 2?", "a": "Proportionally to the marks — Question 1 is worth 20 marks, Question 2 only 10."}

findings.claim: examiners need to see you have addressed both the “analyse” and the “judgements and conclusions” halves of the command
findings.problem: Unevidenced claim about examiner behaviour. The specification states only that part (a) assesses the ability to analyse media products and part (b) the ability to analyse and make judgements and draw conclusions; it says nothing about how answers must be laid out or about what examiners 'need to see'.
findings.correction: Write part (a) and part (b) as clearly separate answers. Part (a) is assessed on analysis of the product; part (b) is assessed on analysis plus judgements and conclusions, so make sure part (b) actually reaches a judgement.

findings.claim: vague answers that could apply to any programme are the most common way marks are lost
findings.problem: Unevidenced assertion about exam frequency and candidate performance; no published board document supports a 'most common' claim for this question.
findings.correction: For Question 2, name the broadcaster, platform or scheduling detail precisely — answers that could apply to any programme cannot show the specific knowledge this question rewards.

findings.claim: The highest-scoring responses consistently make these connections rather than answering each question in isolation.
findings.problem: Unevidenced claim about what high-scoring responses do. The assessment documentation for this section describes the skills assessed (knowledge and understanding of industries and audiences in Question 2) but makes no such statement about top answers.
findings.correction: Linking industry decisions to audience and representation shows a fuller understanding of the framework than treating each area as a separate topic.

findings.claim: Precise, technical language is one of the clearest ways examiners distinguish a secure answer from a vague one.
findings.problem: Unevidenced claim about examiner behaviour; no published board document states this, and no marks are awarded for terminology as such in this section.
findings.correction: Precise, technical language lets you explain meaning accurately and support your points, which is what the analysis questions reward.

findings.claim: You do not need contexts for every answer, but the question papers often invite you to use them.
findings.problem: Unevidenced claim about how often contexts appear. The specification states only that for Question 1 "reference to relevant contexts may be required".
findings.correction: You do not need contexts in every answer, but the specification states that reference to relevant contexts may be required, so be ready to use them.

findings.claim: Naming Propp’s functions or genre theory terms without applying them to a specific moment in a product rarely earns more than the lowest marks.
findings.problem: Unevidenced assertion about how marks are awarded. No published Eduqas GCSE Media Studies document (C680QS, v10, September 2025) states that unapplied theory 'rarely earns more than the lowest marks'; the specification and its tariff descriptors are silent on this. Advice about applying terminology to examples is sound, but it must not be framed as a claim about examiner marking behaviour.
findings.correction: Naming Propp’s functions or genre theory terms is only the starting point — the analysis marks come from applying them to a specific moment in a product.

findings.claim: He called these recurring roles <dfn class="term" ...>character functions</dfn>. ... A seventh role, the sought-for person or prize the hero is working towards, completes Propp’s set.
findings.problem: Minor terminological imprecision. In Morphology of the Folktale (1928) Propp's 'functions' are the 31 recurring plot actions; the seven recurring character roles (villain, donor, helper, princess/sought-for person, dispatcher, hero, false hero) are his 'spheres of action', usually taught as character types. Also, Propp's seventh sphere is normally given as the princess (sought-for person) and her father, so 'completes Propp's set' slightly overstates the tidiness of the list. Unlikely to cost marks at GCSE, where 'character types/functions' is the common usage.
findings.correction: He called these recurring roles character types (Propp's own term is 'spheres of action'; his numbered 'functions' are the recurring plot actions). A seventh role, the sought-for person or prize the hero is working towards, completes the set of character types most often used in media analysis.

findings.claim: since a one-sided answer is capped in the middle bands
findings.problem: Invented marking rule about examiner/mark-band behaviour. No published assessment guidance for this qualification states that a one-sided answer on stereotyping is 'capped in the middle bands', and no assessment rules supplied with this lesson state it. Presenting a fabricated band cap as fact is an unevidenced claim about marking.
findings.correction: For questions on stereotypes, address both sides — their usefulness to producers and audiences, and the problems they create for the groups depicted — so that your answer is balanced rather than one-sided.

findings.claim: This is only one feminist perspective among several; the framework requires you to recognise that feminist approaches to gender and representation are varied, not limited to a single theory.
findings.problem: This asserts a specification requirement that the GCSE theoretical framework does not make. Named academic theories and theorists (including Mulvey's male gaze) are A-level content; the GCSE representation strand requires understanding of how representations of social groups, including gender, are selected and constructed, not knowledge of a range of named feminist theories. Stating that 'the framework requires' this invents a spec obligation.
findings.correction: This is only one feminist perspective among several: feminist approaches to gender and representation are varied, so treat the male gaze as one useful way of analysing a product rather than the only feminist approach.

findings.claim: you are demonstrating exactly the kind of historical and social awareness the higher mark bands reward
findings.problem: Unevidenced claim about how mark bands are awarded; the supplied board context contains no mark-scheme statement that comparison across decades is rewarded in the higher bands.
findings.correction: you are showing awareness of the historical and social contexts in which media products are made, which strengthens an analytical answer.

findings.claim: {"q": "What is one problem stereotypes create for the groups they represent?", "a": "They reinforce power imbalances and remove individuality from real people."}
findings.problem: The question asks for one problem but the answer gives two separate points (reinforcing power imbalances; removing individuality), so it works as a list rather than a single recallable answer. Each point belongs on its own card.
findings.correction: {"q": "What is one problem stereotypes create for the groups they represent?", "a": "They remove individuality by reducing varied real people to a few fixed traits."} (with a separate card: "How can stereotyping affect social power?" / "It can reinforce existing imbalances by limiting how less powerful groups are shown.")

findings.claim: A government-funded broadcaster, such as the BBC in the UK, is paid for through a licence fee rather than relying solely on advertising, which shapes what kind of content it is expected to provide and how it is regulated.
findings.problem: Factually misleading: the BBC is not government-funded. It is a public service broadcaster funded predominantly by UK households through the television licence fee (BBC/UK Parliament research briefing on licence fee funding; the BBC publicly rejected the 'government funded media' label in April 2023). The phrase 'rather than relying solely on advertising' also wrongly implies the BBC's UK services carry some advertising, which they do not.
findings.correction: A publicly funded broadcaster, such as the BBC in the UK, is paid for by households through the television licence fee rather than by advertising, which shapes what kind of content it is expected to provide and how it is regulated.

findings.claim: {"q": "Give an example of a government-funded broadcaster.", "a": "The BBC, funded through the licence fee."}
findings.problem: The card teaches the same factual error as the body text: the BBC is funded by licence-fee payers (households), not by government. A student who writes 'the BBC is government funded' in an exam answer on funding models is making an inaccurate industry claim.
findings.correction: {"q": "Give an example of a publicly funded broadcaster.", "a": "The BBC, funded by households through the television licence fee."}

findings.claim: A broadcaster funded through a government licence fee rather than advertising uses a _____ funding model.
findings.problem: Imprecise terminology, consistent with the error above: the television licence fee is paid by households, not provided by government, so 'government licence fee' / 'government-funded' misdescribes public funding. The distractor set should reflect the standard term 'public funding'.
findings.correction: A broadcaster funded through the television licence fee rather than advertising uses a _____ funding model. (Options: commercial / publicly funded / not-for-profit / convergent — correct: publicly funded)

findings.claim: do not analyse camera work, layout or colour; that earns no credit in this section
findings.problem: Unevidenced claim about marking. No published Eduqas/WJEC GCSE Media Studies document states that references to media language earn 'no credit' in industries questions; the specification and assessment guidance make no such statement. Telling students a whole category of response scores zero is a fabricated marking rule and may discourage relevant, creditworthy material.
findings.correction: When a question asks about media industries in relation to a set product — a newspaper, radio programme, film or video game — keep your answer focused on ownership, funding and regulation rather than drifting into analysis of camera work, layout or colour, which is assessed elsewhere.

findings.claim: Exam answers that connect regulation to ownership and convergence, rather than treating them as separate topics, show the strongest synoptic understanding of the media industries framework.
findings.problem: Unevidenced assertion about what examiners reward. No board document is cited or exists stating that linking these topics produces the 'strongest' answers; this is an invented examiner-preference claim.
findings.correction: Regulation, ownership and convergence are closely connected, so it is useful to be able to explain how a change in one affects the others rather than revising them as separate topics.

findings.claim: Examiners reward answers that apply a need precisely to a specific media product and explain why an audience member might experience it that way
findings.problem: Unevidenced assertion about examiner behaviour/marking preferences. The specification and published assessment criteria for this component state only that learners are assessed on use of relevant subject-specific terminology and relevant theories or theoretical perspectives; they do not state what examiners 'reward' in the terms claimed here.
findings.correction: When a question asks you to analyse or evaluate using Uses and Gratifications theory, naming Blumler and Katz's four needs is not enough on its own. Marks come from applying a need precisely to a specific media product and explaining why an audience member might experience it that way — for example, showing exactly how a scene, feature or article satisfies the entertainment or personal identity need. Two well-applied paragraphs are worth more than five paragraphs that simply list theory.
